title: Prosecutors Cite Comey's Novel as Evidence in Seashell Threat Case, Raising Free Speech Alarms
excerpt: PEN America warns that using a former FBI director's fiction to support criminal charges sets a dangerous precedent for creative expression.
body:
• Federal prosecutors cited James Comey's legal thriller "FDR Drive" as evidence he knew his "86 47" seashell post would be read as a threat against President Trump
  • PEN America called the government's use of fiction in the prosecution a "desperate Hail Mary" that compounds First Amendment concerns
  • Comey's defense team argues the case is vindictive prosecution and that the post did not meet the legal threshold of a true threat
  • Prosecutors disclosed that Iran orchestrated a missile attack on Air Force One in July 2026, citing it among threats justifying the investigation

The Justice Department's prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey over a social media post depicting seashells took an unusual turn this week when prosecutors introduced his own novel as evidence, prompting free-speech advocates to warn the case threatens creative expression nationwide.

In court filings published Tuesday, prosecutors cited Comey's legal thriller "FDR Drive" — a novel about a right-wing podcaster who uses coded language to encourage followers to attack political opponents — as proof that Comey understood how his May 2025 Instagram post would be interpreted.

The Seashell Post and the Novel

The post in question showed seashells arranged on a beach to spell "86 47." The slang term "86" means to remove, get rid of, or refuse service. Trump is the 47th president. Comey has said he found the shells in that arrangement while walking on a North Carolina beach with his wife and interpreted it as a political statement, not a threat.

https://x.com/1109Patricia/status/2090758334408241389

"Citing a novel to save an indictment that is constitutionally dubious is a desperate Hail Mary and should be rejected. A political message, expressed through a photo of seashells, is no true threat."

— Mara Gassmann, Legal Director, PEN America

Prosecutors argued that the novel's plot — in which a charismatic public figure uses public messages to instruct followers to "get rid of" enemies — mirrors what Comey himself did. "On May 15, 2025, a charismatic leader named James Comey posted a coded message to his followers meaning 'kill' or 'get rid of' President Trump," prosecutors wrote, drawing a direct parallel between the novel's fictional villain and Comey.

A Contested Timeline

The filings revealed that Comey's wife sent him a screenshot of a dictionary definition of "86" — meaning "to get rid of or refuse service," not to kill — two minutes before he posted the photo. Prosecutors also highlighted a text Comey sent his literary agent after the post went viral: "Not my intention, but I'll be OK if it sells books."

Comey's defense lawyers have produced evidence that the FBI investigated whether Comey knew of a violent interpretation of "86" from his years prosecuting mob figures in New York and came up empty. They contend the case was brought as retribution for Comey's longstanding criticism of Trump.

The government said there is "no serious dispute" that an objective viewer could read the post as meaning "Kill President Trump," pointing to a slang dictionary entry and reactions from law enforcement officers who flagged the post.

Free Expression at Stake

PEN America, the writers' and free-expression organization, said courts should treat the government's use of Comey's fiction with "extreme caution." The group has advocated for state laws limiting how creative works — lyrics, novels, and other artistic expression — can be used as evidence in criminal cases.

"Americans can distinguish real life from fiction and want the government to respect the right to peacefully advocate for political change," Gassmann said.

The prosecution's broader arguments also referenced multiple threats and assassination attempts against Trump, including what prosecutors described as an Iran-orchestrated missile attack on Air Force One in July 2026.

What's Next

A federal judge will now weigh Comey's motions to dismiss the case on grounds of vindictive prosecution and First Amendment protection. The outcome could set significant precedent for how creative works are treated in criminal proceedings — a question with implications well beyond this case.
